chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from al-Husayn ibn Zarrar, who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and my father asked him about the milk of the dead animal (meitah), the sweat of the dead animal, and the egg of the dead animal, so he said: 'All of this is halal/permissible.'
He said, so I said: 'What about the hair of the pig, which is made into a rope used to draw water from a well from which one drinks and performs ablution?' He said: 'There is no harm in it.'
And Ali ibn Uqbah and Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ribat added in it, saying: 'And the hair and the wool, all of it is halal/permissible.'

key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (ritually pure/permissible)

ai.seo_question: Is the milk and sweat of a dead animal permissible to consume according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Tahdhib al-Ahkam clarifies that bodily excretions and byproducts of *meitah* (animals dying naturally) are ritually pure (*dhakī*), resolving the distinction between the animal's flesh and its functional parts. It specifically addresses the practical jurisprudence of pig hair used in well ropes, affirming its purity for ablution (*wudu*) and drinking, a view supported by the addition of Ali ibn Uqbah and Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ribat. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that impurity (*najāsah*) is primarily inherent in the flesh and blood, while other parts like hair, wool, and milk remain pure unless contaminated by external factors.
